title: Write the Money Rules for Your Relationship
meta_description: Create fair couple money rules for disclosure, spending, debt, investing, family support, safety, emergencies and major financial decisions.

sections.heading: Begin With Decisions, Not a Document
paragraphs: The opening photograph shows two partners working through figures and writing together. That is the point of a money constitution: two adults making visible decisions, not one person presenting finished rules. The document is a practical operating agreement for everyday finances. It is not a loyalty test, a substitute for trust or a legal contract.

Start by naming the decisions that repeatedly create friction. Common examples include how much to save, which debts to attack, what counts as shared spending, when consultation is required and how relatives are supported. A useful constitution answers recurring questions before stress, urgency or a persuasive salesperson controls the answer.

Keep the first version short enough to use. One or two pages can cover purpose, disclosure, shared obligations, personal autonomy, approval thresholds, goals, debt, investing, emergencies, meeting rhythm and amendment. Attach schedules for accounts or goals rather than turning the core agreement into a household encyclopedia nobody will reread.

Write in plain language both partners can explain. Replace “be responsible” with observable actions such as transferring an agreed amount after payday, disclosing new borrowing before application or discussing an unbudgeted purchase above a threshold. Vague virtue words invite different interpretations; operational verbs expose whether the rule can actually be followed.

Treat the constitution as evidence of consent at one moment, not permanent permission. Either partner can raise a safety concern, request a review or decline a new joint liability. The agreement should make discussion easier, but it cannot erase legal ownership, lender terms, tax rules, benefit rules or the right to obtain independent advice.

Use [[S1|MoneyHelper’s guidance on talking with a partner]] to prepare the conversation. Choose a calm time, bring current information and separate facts from character judgments. If discussion is coercive or unsafe, do not use this framework as mediation. Personal safety and confidential specialist support take priority over a joint meeting.

Choose where the document lives and who can edit it. Both partners should be able to retrieve the current version, while changes remain traceable. Avoid a private file controlled by the person who manages the spreadsheet. Shared visibility is a governance control, not an invitation to expose the document publicly.

sections.heading: Map the Financial Household Honestly
paragraphs: Each partner should prepare an individual inventory before combining information. List income, regular bills, annual costs, debt, savings, investments, pensions, insurance, dependants, business interests and commitments to other households. Include account ownership and payment dates. The purpose is shared orientation, not forced transfer of every asset into joint ownership.

Disclose material risks, not every harmless preference. Existing debt, arrears, guarantees, tax obligations, unstable income, credit applications and legal claims can affect shared plans and belong on the table. A small personal purchase may not. Define materiality so privacy and honesty are not falsely treated as opposites.

Reconcile the inventory against statements and contracts. Memory routinely misses subscriptions, annual insurance, buy-now-pay-later plans and family transfers. Use a trailing twelve-month view where possible. Convert irregular costs into monthly amounts, but retain the original due date so a neat average does not hide a near-term cash demand.

Mark ownership and liability separately from who pays. A partner may contribute toward a mortgage without being an owner; a joint borrower may remain liable even after moving out; an app category does not establish legal title. Record uncertainty and seek jurisdiction-specific legal or regulated advice instead of resolving it with household assumptions.

Map unpaid work and care alongside cash. Childcare, elder care, household administration and career sacrifices affect capacity even when no invoice appears. A constitution that recognizes only earnings can reward the person whose paid work depends on another person’s unpaid contribution. Describe both financial and operational responsibilities.

Create one agreed snapshot date and store the inventory securely. Do not put passwords, full card numbers or authentication codes in the constitution. The [[S2|CFPB family-finance preparation guide]] emphasizes that both partners should understand accounts, property, income and bills so either can operate the household if responsibility suddenly shifts.

Do not treat a disclosed balance as self-explanatory. Ask whether the rate can change, whether collateral is involved, whether payments are current and whether another person has rights or claims. Context determines household risk. Record what still needs verification rather than filling gaps with confidence.

sections.heading: State What Money Is Supposed to Protect
paragraphs: Before setting percentages, write three to five household principles. Examples include keeping housing secure, avoiding high-cost revolving debt, preserving each adult’s personal agency, funding children consistently and preparing for income interruption. Principles rank competing demands; they should not become slogans used to end discussion.

Translate every principle into a test. “We value security” might require a minimum emergency reserve and adequate insurance. “We value freedom” might require personal spending that needs no approval. “We support family” might require a defined annual budget rather than open-ended transfers. Tests turn values into decisions without pretending values are mathematical.

Name the trade-offs. More emergency cash can delay investing; faster mortgage repayment can reduce liquidity; a career break can advance care goals while lowering retirement contributions. Record which objective wins in ordinary conditions and which event reopens the decision. Hidden trade-offs later appear as resentment.

Distinguish household goals from individual goals. A deposit, family travel or shared retirement may be joint; education, a business experiment or personal travel may remain individual. Both categories deserve space. Joint life does not require every ambition to merge, but individual plans cannot silently depend on shared cash or another person’s borrowing capacity.

Give goals amount, owner, deadline and next transfer. “Save for a home” is a wish; “build a named deposit fund to a target by a review date” can guide monthly choices. For uncertain goals, use ranges and checkpoints. Do not manufacture precision about future prices, returns or income.

Rank goals in tiers: obligations, resilience, near-term plans and long-term wealth. This prevents a visible but optional purchase from displacing insurance, taxes or an emergency reserve. Revisit priorities after a birth, care need, move, job change or diagnosis. The constitution should preserve purpose while allowing the plan to change.

Add a definition of enough. Without a stopping rule, every goal can demand more and current life is permanently deferred. Define the target or range, what happens after it is reached and which new evidence would justify extending it. Enough is a decision boundary, not a prediction.

sections.heading: Choose Fair Contributions Without Keeping Score
paragraphs: Equal cash contributions are simple when incomes and obligations are similar. They can become punishing when one partner earns less, takes parental leave or performs more unpaid care. Test fairness by examining the share of usable income and the personal money left after contributions, not merely whether the transfers match.

Income-proportional contributions can reflect capacity. Define the denominator: net salary, average variable income, business drawings or all available household income. Decide how tax reserves, maintenance payments and essential disability costs are treated. Recalculate on a schedule rather than turning every payslip into negotiation.

An equal-personal-money approach funds household commitments first and then gives each partner a comparable discretionary amount. It can recognize unpaid care but requires deeper pooling and disclosure. A needs-based approach may fit temporary unemployment, study or illness. No formula is automatically fair; each distributes risk differently.

Record the formula and one worked example. State transfer dates, treatment of bonuses, minimum balances and what happens when income is late. Keep the example illustrative so a pay change does not secretly amend the rule. The formula should be reproducible by both partners without dependence on the household spreadsheet expert.

Do not turn support into an accumulating moral debt. If one partner contributes less cash under the agreed rule, ordinary spending should not require gratitude or permission. Conversely, an income difference does not excuse secrecy or unilateral risk. Fairness combines access, disclosure, workload and future opportunity.

Review contributions after changes in pay, care, health, benefits or dependants. Apply reductions symmetrically where possible and protect basic personal autonomy. A constitution succeeds when it makes adjustment expected rather than humiliating. It fails when an outdated formula becomes leverage against the partner with less current income.

Check the formula against three sample months: normal income, a reduced-income month and a month containing a large annual bill. If the rule repeatedly requires rescue transfers, it is not robust. Adjust timing, buffer or contribution logic before blaming either partner for a design failure.

sections.heading: Give Every Pound a Decision Lane
paragraphs: Create three lanes: shared essentials, shared choices and personal spending. Essentials include agreed housing, utilities, food, care and minimum debt payments. Shared choices include travel, upgrades and optional subscriptions. Personal spending covers items each adult may buy without review. Ambiguous categories should be named before they become arguments.

Assign each lane an account or tracking method only after defining it. One account can support several categories, while many accounts can still conceal a weak plan. Use the fewest structures that preserve legal ownership, safety, tax records and reliable automation. Account design is implementation, not the constitution itself.

Define an approval threshold for unbudgeted shared spending. Below it, either partner may act within the relevant category; above it, both must consent before commitment. Use a lower threshold for recurring obligations than one-time purchases because a subscription or loan creates future claims on income.

Add a waiting period for non-essential large decisions. Twenty-four or seventy-two hours gives both people time to check the goal, total cost, financing and alternatives. The rule applies to attractive investments and family requests as well as purchases. Urgency created by a seller is not a household emergency.

Clarify reimbursements. If a partner pays a shared cost personally, specify how it is recorded and repaid. Frequent reimbursement queues signal that the structure is underfunded or poorly assigned. Do not let the person with the larger credit limit become the household’s involuntary working-capital provider.

Preserve a no-explanation personal amount. Autonomy reduces petty surveillance and makes boundaries credible. The amount must not be used to hide material debt or evade shared obligations, but the other partner should not audit ordinary purchases. Privacy within an agreed limit is different from financial secrecy.

Assign responsibility for category maintenance. Someone must update annual costs, remove ended subscriptions and confirm that automated transfers still match the plan. Rotate or review this work. A lane that is never reconciled gradually becomes a story about spending rather than an accurate control.

sections.heading: Set Debt and Credit Rules Before Borrowing
paragraphs: List each debt by legal borrower, balance, rate, minimum, term, security and purpose. Then state whether repayment is individual, shared or partly supported. A household choice to help does not necessarily change contractual liability. Keep records and obtain advice before refinancing individual debt into a joint or secured obligation.

Create a disclosure rule for new credit. Any joint application, guarantee, secured borrowing or debt that could disrupt shared goals requires advance discussion. A personal credit card within a defined limit may require periodic balance disclosure rather than approval. Missed payments, arrears and collection contact require immediate disclosure regardless of amount.

Ban borrowing to conceal a budget gap. If routine costs need credit, revise contributions, spending or income assumptions. Moving a balance can change interest and timing but does not repair negative cash flow. Protect housing, utilities, food, taxes and essential transport before optional goals when money is short.

Agree a repayment priority rather than improvising after every statement. Compare interest, promotional expiry, security, penalties and psychological benefits. Preserve a minimum emergency buffer so one repair does not recreate expensive debt. Any deviation should have an amount, reason and review date.

Treat guarantees and co-signing as full-risk decisions. Model the payment if the primary borrower pays nothing, plus effects on future borrowing and relationships. Affection does not reduce contractual exposure. Each partner should be free to obtain independent advice before putting shared assets or income behind someone else’s promise.

Define what happens after a breach: disclose facts, stop new borrowing, protect essentials, contact creditors early and seek reputable debt advice. Avoid punishment rules that make concealment more likely. Accountability means repairing the system and trust while preserving safety, not giving one partner indefinite control over the other.

Keep credit reports and contractual records individual even when discussion is shared. Each person should obtain information through legitimate channels and correct errors directly. The constitution can require material disclosure, but it should not authorize identity impersonation, unauthorized applications or routine handling of another adult’s private credentials.

sections.heading: Turn Big Purchases Into a Repeatable Process
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows a couple signing documents in front of a professional. It makes the risk visible: a major decision can become binding in minutes. The constitution should slow the household before property, vehicles, business funding, guarantees or long contracts convert optimism into fixed obligations.

Use a decision brief for purchases above the agreed threshold. Record purpose, full price, financing cost, ongoing expenses, ownership, exit cost, effect on other goals and worst affordable month. Include at least one alternative and a no-purchase option. Monthly payment alone is never the full price.

Separate research from consent. One partner may gather quotes, but both should receive the same final documents and enough time to review them. A salesperson, adviser or family member does not replace household agreement. Independent advice may be necessary when incentives, law or technical complexity matter.

Confirm whose name appears on title, loan, warranty, insurance and recurring bills. Contribution does not always create ownership, and ownership does not always eliminate liability. Record the intended arrangement and obtain legal advice where property rights, marriage, inheritance or separation could produce a different result.

Stress-test the decision against lower income, higher rates, repair costs and delayed resale. Do not simply ask whether the normal payment fits today. Ask what would be cut, who bears the administrative burden and how long reserves last. A purchase that consumes every contingency is not affordable merely because approval is available.

Schedule a post-purchase review. Verify registrations, beneficiaries, insurance, payment dates, refunds, tax records and the impact on savings. Large commitments create follow-up work that marketing rarely shows. The decision is complete only when the household can operate and exit it as intended.

Use cooling-off and cancellation rights where available, but never assume they exist. Verify deadlines and required delivery methods in the actual agreement. Save the signed version and evidence of notices. A household process should not depend on recovering from a rushed signature after the legal window closes.

sections.heading: Write an Investment Rule Both Can Defend
paragraphs: State the goal, horizon, required liquidity and acceptable loss before naming investments. Partners can have different emotional tolerance, but shared money needs an agreed risk budget. The [[S3|Investor.gov allocation guide]] links asset mix to time horizon and risk tolerance and explains diversification and rebalancing.

Decide which investments are shared and which remain individual. Shared goals need transparent contributions, ownership and withdrawal authority. Individual retirement accounts may remain legally personal while affecting the household plan. Do not exchange passwords or informally trade in another person’s account.

Choose an allocation range, contribution schedule and rebalancing rule. Ranges avoid constant tinkering while limiting drift. Define whether new contributions, calendar reviews or threshold breaches trigger rebalancing. Record exceptions for near-term goals that need cash or lower volatility.

Prohibit leverage, concentrated bets or complex products in shared funds unless both partners understand the maximum loss, costs, liquidity and tax consequences and explicitly amend the rule. Fear of missing out is not consent. A product’s availability inside an app does not make it suitable.

Set adviser and platform checks. Verify registration where applicable, understand fees and incentives, retain statements and use each owner’s legitimate credentials. Neither partner should authorize transfers from shared reserves during a live sales call. Fraud prevention is part of household governance.

Measure progress against contributions, allocation and goal dates—not the other partner’s predictions. Market outcomes are uncertain. A constitution should control behavior the household can repeat: saving, diversification, costs, review and fraud resistance. It should not promise returns or turn temporary underperformance into personal blame.

If risk preferences differ, locate the disagreement. It may concern goal timing, job stability, emergency reserves or emotional capacity rather than investment knowledge. Solve the underlying constraint where possible. Splitting the difference mechanically can produce a portfolio neither partner understands nor can hold through loss.

sections.heading: Protect Autonomy and Recognize Economic Abuse
paragraphs: Consent requires practical ability to say no. Each adult should retain lawful access to identification, communication, essential money and a payment route. A shared plan that leaves one person unable to buy necessities, travel safely or obtain advice is not efficient governance; it is dangerous dependency.

Economic abuse can include controlling accounts, sabotaging work, demanding credentials, taking credit in another person’s name or forcing explanations for every purchase. The [[S4|UK government economic-abuse toolkit]] describes control over money and resources as abuse. A constitution must never normalize these behaviors as transparency.

Use separate credentials and strong authentication. Shared ownership should be established through the provider, not by impersonation or password sharing. Review recovery email, phone access, statements and connected devices. Each legitimate user needs their own auditable route into joint services.

Set privacy boundaries. Partners can require disclosure of material liabilities and shared-goal progress without inspecting every personal transaction. Alerts should protect against fraud and missed bills, not create constant surveillance. If one partner uses monitoring to intimidate or restrict, a joint meeting may increase risk.

Include a safety override: either person can pause a non-essential joint transaction and seek independent advice. This does not permit abandoning essential obligations or hiding assets. It creates breathing room where pressure, misunderstanding or compromised security is suspected.

Where abuse or immediate danger may exist, prioritize confidential specialist help, a safe device and local emergency options. Do not rely on the constitution, couples counseling or mediation to equalize coercive power. Preserve evidence only where safe and obtain legal, banking and support advice appropriate to the jurisdiction.

sections.heading: Plan for Children, Relatives and Care
paragraphs: Define which dependant costs are household obligations: childcare, education, healthcare, activities, support from previous relationships and elder care. Vague goodwill often creates recurring conflict. Assign funding, approval and records while protecting children’s and relatives’ privacy.

Set boundaries for gifts and family loans. Decide an annual amount, approval threshold and whether repayment is expected. If repayment matters, document terms and assess affordability as if the money may never return. Do not lend emergency reserves or borrow jointly to preserve appearances.

Discuss cultural and intergenerational expectations directly. Regular remittances, ceremonies, housing support and caregiving can be core values rather than discretionary extras. Recognizing importance does not remove limits. Put the commitment in the budget so it competes honestly with other goals.

Account for care work. A partner who reduces paid employment may lose current income, pension contributions, advancement and bargaining power. Decide how personal spending, retirement saving, insurance and re-entry costs will be supported. “We will manage” is not a plan for an unequal economic sacrifice.

Agree how children learn about money without making them referees. Age-appropriate participation can cover saving, spending and household trade-offs, but children should not carry adult debt anxiety or relay messages between partners. Keep conflict and confidential balances out of their role.

Review the plan when care needs change. A diagnosis, school transition, new child or ageing parent can alter time and cash simultaneously. Reprioritize rather than quietly expecting one person to absorb the shortfall. Obtain benefit, employment, tax and legal guidance where local rules matter.

sections.heading: Run Money Meetings That Produce Decisions
paragraphs: Use a fixed rhythm: a short monthly operations meeting and a deeper quarterly review. The monthly agenda covers cash, upcoming bills, goal transfers, exceptions and assigned actions. The quarterly review covers net position, risks, investments, insurance and amendments. A calendar protects the conversation from occurring only during crises.

Share preparation. Rotate who produces the dashboard, checks statements or records actions. The partner who enjoys spreadsheets should not automatically carry every renewal, dispute and form. Administrative labor is real household work and should be visible in the constitution.

Begin with variances, not accusations. Say the category exceeded plan, a transfer was late or the reserve fell below its floor. Then identify cause, effect and next action. Character judgments make accurate disclosure less likely. Operational language keeps the meeting focused without excusing repeated concealment.

Create a decision log with date, choice, amount, owner and review point. Record dissent where useful. The log prevents memory contests and shows whether exceptions are becoming the real policy. It should not become a dossier of minor mistakes or a weapon in unrelated arguments.

Time-box unresolved issues. If facts are missing, assign research and reconvene. If values conflict, identify the smallest reversible experiment. If legal or regulated advice is required, pause commitment. Exhaustion is not agreement, and continuing until one person surrenders is not a sound decision process.

End by confirming the next three actions and who owns them. Send both partners the same record in a secure shared location. The meeting is successful when decisions become executable and both people remain informed—not when every financial topic is solved in one sitting.

sections.heading: Design Emergency Authority Without Sharing Passwords
paragraphs: The late photograph shows another couple jointly reviewing bills and written records. It makes continuity tangible: either partner should be able to understand essential payments if the other is ill, travelling or unavailable. Familiarity must come from proper access and documentation, not from borrowing someone else’s login.

Create an emergency map listing providers, account purpose, bill dates, advisers, insurance contacts and document locations. Omit passwords and full security credentials. Use a reputable password manager, provider-authorized access and formal legal authority where appropriate. Tell the other person how recovery works and test it safely.

Name immediate priorities for an income shock: housing, food, utilities, healthcare, care, insurance and essential transport. Identify which discretionary transfers pause automatically and when creditors are contacted. A pre-agreed sequence reduces panic while leaving room for actual circumstances.

Maintain a reserve rule with target range, permitted uses and replenishment order. Distinguish emergencies from predictable irregular expenses such as annual premiums or repairs. A sinking fund handles expected timing; the emergency reserve handles genuine shocks. Do not invest the portion that must remain immediately available.

Address incapacity and death with qualified advice. Account mandates, powers of attorney, wills, nominations and insurance have jurisdiction-specific effects. A household note does not create legal authority. The constitution should prompt proper documents and record where current originals and professional contacts are kept.

Test continuity once a year. The backup partner should locate a bill, explain the next month’s cash flow and identify emergency contacts without moving money unnecessarily. Repair access gaps while both are well. Resilience is not distrust; it is protection against one person becoming a single point of household failure.

sections.heading: Amend the Rules When Life Changes
paragraphs: Put a version number, adoption date and next review date on the constitution. List automatic review triggers: major pay changes, new debt, marriage, separation, a child, care responsibilities, relocation, property purchase, business start, illness or retirement. Review does not mean every rule must change.

Use a simple amendment process. State the proposed change, reason, financial effect, start date and next checkpoint. Both partners receive time to review. Temporary changes should expire or be renewed explicitly so crisis measures do not become permanent through inertia.

Keep prior versions and decision records securely. History helps explain account structures, contributions and promises, but it does not override law or establish ownership by itself. Do not edit old records to make current expectations appear longstanding.

When a rule is repeatedly broken, diagnose design before adding punishment. The threshold may be unrealistic, income may be unstable, categories may be unclear or one person may lack access. Deliberate concealment still requires accountability, but stronger surveillance may worsen safety and trust.

If the relationship ends, switch from shared optimization to lawful stabilization. Preserve statements, protect essential payments, avoid hiding or destroying records and seek independent legal advice promptly. A constitution can identify accounts and intentions, but it cannot settle property, support, custody, debt or tax rights.

The final test is practical: can both partners explain the rules, operate the system, question a decision and leave unsafe arrangements? A good money constitution does not eliminate disagreement. It gives ordinary disagreement a fair process, keeps major risks visible and changes before outdated promises damage the household.

Schedule a first review soon after adoption rather than waiting a year. Thirty or sixty days reveals ambiguous categories, impractical thresholds and missing responsibilities while changes are still easy. Record what worked as well as what failed. A constitution should preserve useful behavior, not create constant revision for its own sake.

summary: A couple’s money constitution is a short operating agreement for recurring financial decisions. It is not a legal contract or proof of commitment. It should make consent, responsibility, autonomy and review visible before stress or sales pressure determines the outcome.

Begin with separate inventories of income, bills, annual costs, debt, savings, investments, insurance, dependants and other commitments. Mark legal ownership and liability separately from who pays. Verify material facts against statements and contracts while keeping passwords and authentication codes outside the document.

Write a few household principles and convert each into a test. Security may require a reserve; autonomy may require personal spending; family support may require a defined budget. Name trade-offs so one goal does not quietly displace another.

Choose a contribution method both partners can reproduce: equal cash, income-proportional, equal personal money or a temporary needs-based approach. Include unpaid care and career sacrifices. Record transfer dates, treatment of variable income and review triggers rather than treating today’s incomes as permanent.

Separate shared essentials, shared choices and personal spending. Define ambiguous categories and set approval thresholds for unbudgeted commitments. Recurring contracts deserve a lower threshold than one-time purchases. Preserve a personal amount that does not require routine explanation.

List debts by legal borrower and terms, then state how repayment is handled. Require advance discussion for joint credit, guarantees and secured borrowing. Missed payments and arrears need prompt disclosure. Never use new borrowing to hide an ordinary cash-flow deficit.

For major purchases, prepare a decision brief covering total cost, financing, ownership, ongoing expenses, effect on goals, worst affordable month and exit route. Both partners should review final documents without seller-created urgency and obtain independent advice where necessary.

Shared investing needs a goal, time horizon, liquidity requirement, risk budget, allocation range, contribution schedule and rebalancing rule. Avoid leverage or complex products unless both partners understand maximum loss, costs and liquidity and expressly amend the agreement.

Protect autonomy. Each adult needs lawful access to identification, communication, essential money and a payment route. Use separate credentials and provider-authorized access. Material transparency does not justify transaction-by-transaction surveillance, forced borrowing or control of employment.

Define responsibilities for children, relatives and care, including funding, approval and records. Recognize the retirement and career effects of unpaid care. Put family support inside the budget rather than relying on open-ended promises or lending emergency reserves.

Hold short monthly operating meetings and deeper quarterly reviews. Rotate preparation, record decisions and use neutral language about variances. Time-box unresolved issues and pause commitments when facts, consent or professional advice are missing.

Create an emergency map of providers, bills, insurance and document locations without exposing passwords. Define reserve uses and which transfers pause during an income shock. Obtain proper legal documents for incapacity and death; a household note cannot create authority.

Version the constitution and amend it after major life changes. Temporary changes need expiry dates. Preserve records, but remember the document cannot determine legal ownership, debt liability, tax or separation rights. The best system can be explained, operated and challenged by both partners.

Keep the current document in a secure location both partners can reach, with traceable edits and no passwords. Add worked examples for contribution and approval rules, and test them against normal, reduced-income and annual-bill months before relying on them.

Consent must remain reversible before a commitment is made. Use waiting periods, verify cancellation terms and permit independent advice. If discussion involves intimidation, forced debt, restricted access or surveillance, stop treating the issue as ordinary budgeting and seek safe specialist support.
Review the first version after thirty or sixty days. Keep useful rules, clarify ambiguity and assign missing work. The goal is stable, understandable governance—not endless editing.

faq.question: Is a couple money constitution legally binding?
faq.answer: Usually it is a practical household agreement, not a substitute for contracts or legal advice. Ownership, debt, tax and separation rights depend on documents and local law.

faq.question: Must couples combine every account?
faq.answer: No. Joint, separate or hybrid structures can all work. Choose ownership and access according to purpose, safety, liability and agreed responsibilities.

faq.question: What spending threshold should we use?
faq.answer: Set an amount proportionate to your cash flow, with a lower threshold for recurring commitments. Review it after income or household costs change.

faq.question: How should unequal incomes be handled?
faq.answer: Compare equal contributions, income-proportional shares, equal personal money and needs-based arrangements. Include unpaid care and remaining personal autonomy.

faq.question: Should partners share banking passwords?
faq.answer: No. Use provider-authorized joint access and separate credentials. Store emergency information securely and use formal authority for incapacity where appropriate.

faq.question: What if one partner hides debt?
faq.answer: Protect essentials, obtain complete facts, stop new borrowing, contact creditors or reputable advice early, and rebuild rules and trust without coercive surveillance.

faq.question: How often should the constitution be reviewed?
faq.answer: Use monthly operating meetings, quarterly deeper reviews and trigger reviews after major income, debt, care, property, health or relationship changes.

glossary.definition: Financial information significant enough to affect shared obligations, risk or goals.
The amount or commitment above which joint approval is required.
Practical ability to use agreed personal resources without routine permission or surveillance.
A contractual responsibility shared by more than one borrower or account holder.
Money accumulated gradually for a predictable future expense.
Liquid money held for significant unexpected financial disruption.
Ability and willingness to accept investment loss or volatility.
Control or restriction of another person’s money or economic resources.
A dated record of major choices, owners, actions and review points.
An event that requires the household rules to be reconsidered.
